common_name: Martha Hitchcock Azalea (White Purple-Picotee Glenn Dale Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Martha Hitchcock is a Glenn Dale Hybrid bred for hardiness beyond the tender Southern Indian Hybrids while retaining a large, showy flower.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Martha Hitchcock is one of the most recognizable Glenn Dale Hybrid azaleas, part of the group bred by USDA horticulturist Benjamin Yeo Morrison at the Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station in Maryland from the 1930s through the 1950s to combine cold hardiness with the large flowers of tender Asian azalea species. Its large (up to 4-inch), broad white flowers are strikingly edged with a wide band of vivid reddish-purple to magenta along each wavy petal margin, a bold picotee pattern that makes it stand out from solid-colored azaleas. The plant forms an upright, well-branched, semi-evergreen to evergreen shrub reaching 3-5 feet, blooming in mid-to-late spring in a single heavy flush. Named for Martha Bowers Hitchcock, a Washington-area horticultural patron, it remains a benchmark bicolor selection among Glenn Dale cultivars and is still sought out by azalea collectors and public gardens. Water deeply during dry spells, keep mulch over the shallow root zone, and prune only right after bloom since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Glenn Dale Hybrid Documentation

common_name: Ben Morrison Azalea (Orange-Red White-Edged Glenn Dale Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ben Morrison is a vigorous, cold-hardier Glenn Dale Hybrid named for the breeder who created the entire group.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Ben Morrison is a Glenn Dale Hybrid azalea named posthumously in honor of Benjamin Yeo Morrison, the USDA plant breeder who developed the entire Glenn Dale group at the Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station between the 1930s and 1950s to extend azalea hardiness northward while keeping large, showy flowers. Its bold, wide-flaring flowers are a vivid orange-red to red-orange with a narrow, irregular white picotee margin along the petal edges, giving each bloom a striking bicolor contrast. Plants form a dense, rounded, semi-evergreen to evergreen mound 3-5 feet tall, flowering in mid-spring in one heavy display. As one of the flagship cultivars of the group, it is frequently used to illustrate the vigor and color range Morrison achieved by crossing hardy Korean and Japanese azalea species with showier tender Asian forms. Water deeply during dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool, and prune only right after bloom since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Glenn Dale Hybrid Documentation

common_name: Louise Gable Azalea (Double Salmon-Pink Gable Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Louise Gable is an older, exceptionally cold-hardy Gable hybrid well suited to the cooler edge of the evergreen azalea range as well as the Gulf Coast.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Louise Gable, bred by Pennsylvania hybridizer Joseph B. Gable, is a longtime favorite among the Gable hybrid azaleas prized for their exceptional cold hardiness relative to Southern Indian Hybrids. It bears profuse, hose-in-hose (double, flower-within-a-flower) blooms in a warm salmon-pink shade with a deeper rose-red blotch, opening in a heavy mid-spring flush over dense, twiggy, semi-evergreen foliage. The compact, mounding habit (3-3.5 feet) and reliable heavy bloom make it a dependable choice for foundation plantings, woodland edges, and mixed shrub borders. As one of Gable's most widely propagated introductions, it helped establish the Gable hybrids as a hardier alternative to tender Southern Indicas for gardeners north of the Deep South, while still performing well through Gulf Coast heat and humidity. Water deeply during dry periods, keep mulch over the shallow root zone, and prune only right after flowering since next year's buds set soon afterward.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Girard's Crimson Azalea (Deep Red Compact Girard Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Girard's Crimson is a compact, cold-hardy Girard hybrid valued for true-red flower color and good winter foliage bronzing.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Girard's Crimson was developed by Ohio nurseryman Peter Girard Sr. as part of his line of cold-hardy, compact evergreen azaleas bred for northern landscapes as well as warmer regions. It produces abundant, true deep-red flowers in mid-spring over small, glossy, dark green leaves that take on a rich reddish-purple cast in cold weather, adding cool-season interest after bloom. The dense, low-mounding habit (2-3 feet) makes it well suited to foundation plantings, mass plantings, and smaller garden spaces where larger Southern Indica types would quickly overwhelm the bed. Girard hybrids as a group were bred to combine the compact habit and hardiness of Kurume-type azaleas with improved flower size and color saturation. Water deeply during dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool, and prune only right after flowering since next year's buds set soon afterward.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Boule de Neige Rhododendron (Compact White-Flowered Hardy Hybrid Rhododendron)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Boule de Neige is an old, exceptionally cold-hardy and heat-tolerant hybrid that adapts well across a wide climate range.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Boule de Neige is a classic French hardy hybrid (its name translates to "snowball") introduced in the late 1870s from Catawbiense and Caucasicum rhododendron parentage. Dense, rounded trusses of pure white flowers with a faint greenish-yellow throat blush open in late spring against glossy, dark evergreen foliage on a compact, rounded shrub. It has long been valued by American gardeners for a rare combination of extreme cold hardiness and unusually good heat and humidity tolerance for a white-flowered hybrid, allowing it to succeed from cold northern gardens down into warmer transitional zones where many large-leaved rhododendrons struggle. Its dense, well-branched habit and reliable bloom have kept it in commerce for well over a century as a dependable specimen or mass-planting choice. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Olga Mezitt Rhododendron (Rosy-Pink Cold-Hardy PJM Group Rhododendron)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Olga Mezitt is an exceptionally cold-hardy PJM-group selection that tolerates more sun than most large-leaved rhododendrons.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Olga Mezitt is a selection from Weston Nurseries in Massachusetts within the same cold-hardy PJM breeding line, named for the wife of nursery founder Edmund V. Mezitt. It bears clear, rosy-pink flowers slightly larger than straight PJM, opening in early to mid-spring over small, aromatic, dark green leaves that turn a deep plum-mahogany in cold weather for strong winter interest. Compared to standard PJM, Olga Mezitt tends to grow a bit larger and shows good tolerance of heat and humidity in addition to its parent line's renowned cold hardiness, making it a versatile choice from northern gardens into warmer transitional zones. Mulch to keep roots cool, avoid heavy or poorly drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Vulcan Rhododendron (Bright Red Hardy Hybrid Rhododendron)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Vulcan is a classic English hardy hybrid valued for its bright, true-red flower color.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Vulcan is a mid-20th-century English hardy hybrid rhododendron bred by John Waterer, Sons and Crisp, prized for producing large, rounded trusses of bright, glowing red flowers in mid-to-late spring over broad, dark evergreen leaves. Its dense, well-branched, rounded habit and dependable heavy bloom have kept it a standard red-flowered choice among hardy hybrid rhododendrons for decades, valued as a strong companion to purple- and white-flowered cultivars like Boule de Neige, Nova Zembla, and Blue Peter in mixed rhododendron plantings. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells since shallow-rooted rhododendrons are sensitive to drought, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Blue Peter Rhododendron (Lavender-Blue Dark-Blotched Hardy Hybrid Rhododendron)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Blue Peter is a classic English hardy hybrid grown for its ruffled lavender-blue flowers with a bold dark blotch.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Blue Peter, introduced by John Waterer, Sons and Crisp in the early 1930s, is one of the most widely grown English hardy hybrid rhododendrons. Large, frilled trusses of pale lavender-blue to lilac flowers, each marked with a bold, near-black purple blotch and ruffled petal edges, open in late spring over broad, dark evergreen foliage on a vigorous, upright-rounded shrub. Its striking bicolor flower and dependable vigor have kept it a garden and show standard for nearly a century, frequently used as an anchor specimen in rhododendron borders and woodland gardens. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells since shallow-rooted rhododendrons are sensitive to drought, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Mrs. Furnival Rhododendron (Pink Maroon-Blotched Compact Hardy Hybrid Rhododendron)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Mrs. Furnival is a compact, widely admired English hardy hybrid noted for its clean pink flower and prominent maroon blotch.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Mrs. Furnival, introduced by John Waterer, Sons and Crisp in 1920, is regarded as one of the finest hardy hybrid rhododendrons for garden and exhibition use. Rounded trusses of clear pale pink flowers, each marked with a distinct dark red-brown to maroon blotch on the upper petal, open in late spring over dense, dark green foliage on a compact, well-shaped, rounded shrub. Its refined flower color combination, dependable bud hardiness, and tidy habit have earned it an Award of Garden Merit from the Royal Horticultural Society and made it a long-standing favorite for foundation and specimen planting in shaded borders. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells since shallow-rooted rhododendrons are sensitive to drought, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Chinzan is a late-blooming Satsuki azalea popular for bonsai as well as border and container planting.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Chinzan is a traditional Japanese Satsuki azalea cultivar prized for its deep, saturated wine-purple to reddish-purple flowers with a slightly darker throat, opening several weeks later than most Southern Indica and Kurume azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer. Its compact, twiggy growth habit, small glossy leaves, and tolerance of heavy pruning have made it one of the most widely used Satsuki cultivars in bonsai culture, where it is trained and shown for both its floral display and refined branch structure, though it performs equally well as an unpruned landscape or container shrub. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds set soon after bloom ends on this later-flowering type.

common_name: Shinnyo-no-Tsuki Azalea (Giant White Pink-Streaked Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Shinnyo-no-Tsuki is a late-blooming Satsuki azalea celebrated for its unusually large, variably patterned flowers, popular in bonsai and specimen culture.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Shinnyo-no-Tsuki ("moon of true suchness") is a celebrated Japanese Satsuki azalea cultivar known for exceptionally large flowers, often 3 inches or more across, that open predominantly white but are streaked, flecked, or sectored with varying amounts of pink to magenta in a highly unpredictable pattern from flower to flower and even year to year on the same plant. Like other Satsuki cultivars it blooms several weeks later than most Southern Indica and Kurume azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer, and its compact, twiggy habit and tolerance of heavy pruning make it a favorite subject for bonsai as well as container and border planting where its dramatic, ever-changing flower display can be appreciated up close. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds set soon after bloom ends on this later-flowering type.

common_name: Ramapo Rhododendron (Dwarf Lavender-Blue Cold-Hardy Small-Leaf Rhododendron)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ramapo is an exceptionally cold-hardy dwarf rhododendron well suited to rock gardens and small-space plantings.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ramapo was bred by New Jersey hybridizer Guy Nearing from small-leaved, extremely cold-hardy Rhododendron species parentage in the same lineage that produced the PJM group. It forms a dense, mounding dwarf shrub of small, gray-green leaves that take on a plum-purple cast in winter, smothered in early spring with abundant small, vivid lavender-blue to violet flowers. Its compact size and outstanding cold hardiness make Ramapo especially well suited to rock gardens, foundation plantings, and small residential landscapes where larger rhododendrons would be impractical. Mulch to keep roots cool, avoid heavy or poorly drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.
